current_paragraph: Nicaragua's money is issued by the Central Bank of Nicaragua, which scores 31 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. One case runs from 2000 to 2008 and ended in an official finding. In 2007 the country's Comptroller General, the state auditor, concluded that the bank's board sold CENI certificates, paper issued to cover the collapse of banks, for less than they were worth and then raised interest rates to the benefit of the main buyer, Bancentro; the fraud is put at 500 million dollars. The Comptroller alleged criminal involvement by six men, among them former finance minister Eduardo Montealegre, who denied wrongdoing and called it a political witch hunt, and in July 2008 a special prosecutor filed charges against 39 people including him. No central bank officials are named among the accused and no court ruling is given, though former bank president Francisco Mayorga had already been found guilty in the banking scandal. The man who now runs the bank came to it from the government: Ovidio Reyes was Chief Economist at the Ministry of Finance from 2004 to 2012, became the bank's General Manager in 2012-13 and its President in January 2014, a move between two public bodies, with no private employer named. At the end of 2024 the statute governing the bank was rewritten in a week. The presidency sent the National Assembly the Ley de Administracion del Sistema Monetario y Financiero on 19 December 2024; it went to committee on 23 December during the legislative recess, was approved on 26 December and published in La Gaceta on 30 December. It repealed the bank's own organic law and the law governing the Superintendency of Banks and Other Financial Institutions, and put the two institutions, until then independent of each other, under one statute and one common board chaired by Reyes, abolishing the Superintendency's own board; Reyes was also given coordination of the Financial Analysis Unit and the deposit fund. The law's own text says the institutions keep organic, functional, administrative, financial and budgetary autonomy and their institutional specialisation. Divergentes read it the other way, writing that the law eliminates the autonomy of the monetary and financial institutions and gives plenipotentiary powers to Reyes and to the Executive, and that removing the cross-checks between supervisor and central bank removes a safeguard against political and economic bias. Article 24 obliges every person resident or domiciled in Nicaragua, national or foreign, to give the bank and the Superintendency whatever economic, financial, statistical and regulatory information they ask for. The bank did not object publicly and its president gained authority rather than losing it; what changed was that the law governing the bank was rewritten by the Executive, without consultation. Baker Tilly Nicaragua, S.A. audited the accounts for 2024, and on 27 March 2024 the printer Orell Fussli was reported to have been partly awarded a tender to print and supply the bank's banknotes, with no value or quantity given.

current_paragraph: The Central Bank of the Congo issues the country's money. In April 2021 a report by Congo's state finance inspectorate, the IGF, called a 43 million US dollar transfer from a central bank account at BGFI Bank to the food importer Egal an embezzlement of public funds, and said the bank kept false accounts to cover it: its 2013 accounts showed about 43.1 million dollars in that account when the real balance was about 119,000 dollars. The former governor Deogratias Mutombo, the bank and PricewaterhouseCoopers did not respond to the journalists who reported this from leaked BGFI documents. On 25 October 2023 the accounts of Mutombo and of Albert Yuma, former board chairman of the mining company Gecamines, were frozen over an alleged embezzlement of 25.521 million dollars, with both men required to remain available to the national audit court; that allegation is unproven and still under investigation. Belgium's federal prosecutor also opened a money laundering investigation into Mutombo and five others, with searches in September 2023; as of October 2024 the prosecutor said no suspect had been charged. The bank scores 34 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Giesecke+Devrient printed the 200-franc note issued on 31 July 2007. The bank's accounts are audited by Ernst & Young RDC of Kinshasa, which gave an unqualified opinion on the year ended 31 December 2024. In a communique that reached the state news agency ACP on Wednesday 23 September 2026 the Cour des comptes, Congo's audit court, announced an audit mission at the Banque Centrale du Congo to examine the bank's treasury operations for the 2025 financial year, as part of checking how the 2025 finance law was carried out. The court's First President, Jimmy Munganga, instructed the bank's services to hand the auditors the documents they need. No start or end date is given, and parliament's review of the 2025 accounts-settlement bill and of the 2027 finance bill waits on the court filing its report.

current_paragraph: Lesotho issues the loti, and the South African rand circulates alongside it. Under the Common Monetary Area, which replaced a Rand Monetary Area agreement signed in December 1974 and was followed by a Multilateral Monetary Agreement in February 1992 when Namibia joined, member currencies are pegged to the rand one for one and are legal tender only in the country that issues them; Lesotho must back what it issues fully with rand assets, and South Africa pays it an imputed return on rand circulating there. All five of its current notes, introduced on 23 December 2021, are printed by De La Rue. In February 2024 three South Africans appeared in the Ficksburg Magistrates Court on fraud and money laundering charges over 57 million rand said to have been stolen from the Central Bank of Lesotho. The Hawks, a South African police unit, said Lesotho officials intercepted vouchers meant for service providers and diverted the payments to co-conspirators in South Africa, and that some officials were already before court in Lesotho. The charges are unproven. Its 2023 accounts were audited by Moteane, Quashie & Associates with SizweNtsalubaGobodo Grant Thornton. Lesotho scores 32 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and corruption and secrecy around the bank is its weakest side, at 60. At a hearing on Monday 8 June 2026, at which the Auditor General presented consolidated financial statements for 31 March 2023 and 2024, the parliamentary Public Accounts Committee called for a forensic audit of the Central Bank of Lesotho to trace missing public money. Its chairperson, Machabana Lemphane-Letsie, said the bank must undergo a forensic audit and say who the money had been paid to. The figures in the report do not agree with each other: its headline puts the gap at M3.9 billion, while the statements it describes show government cash of M5.91 billion at 31 March 2024 against M2.82 billion in the consolidated accounts, a difference of M3.09 billion, which a quotation in the same piece also gives. The committee resolved that the Auditor General's office submit a budget for the audit by 30 June; that office said it has neither the expertise nor any budget allocated for one. The bank resisted, citing its own 2000 Act, which provides for an external auditor and limits the Auditor General to auditing currency balances rather than government payments the bank makes for the state.

Common Monetary Area (common monetary area)

The Rand Monetary Area agreement was signed in December 1974 by South Africa, Swaziland and Lesotho; it was replaced by the Common Monetary Area in July 1986 and by the Multilateral Monetary Agreement in February 1992, when Namibia formally joined.
Member currencies have been pegged to the rand at par since their introduction; they are legal tender only in the issuing country.
Lesotho and Namibia must fully back their currency issues with rand assets; Eswatini does not face this requirement.
The rand has not been de jure legal tender in Eswatini since 1986.
South Africa makes compensatory payments representing an imputed return on rand circulating as legal tender in Lesotho and Namibia; Eswatini has received none since 1986.

Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and Finance Minister Chrystia Freeland both publicly defended the bank's independence, and former governor David Dodge rejected the criticism. The party's own finance critic, Ed Fast, was removed from that role after saying publicly that the pledge was deeply troubling and hurt the party's economic credibility.
